newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Delay to Yeltsin surgery entails political risks.
newsitem.headline: Delay to Yeltsin surgery entails political risks.

text.p: The prospect of a long delay in President Boris Yeltsin's planned heart operation may reduce the medical dangers but it raises the risk of far-reaching political complications, Russian analysts said on Monday.

Since Yeltsin disappeared from public view shortly before he was re-elected last July, more than his own health has been under scrutiny. The condition of Russia's entire political system, dominated by the president, has been in question.

Jostling for influence in the Kremlin has intensified in Yeltsin's absence and looks set to continue if, as suggested by one of his surgeons on Sunday, his bypass operation is delayed by more than six weeks or cancelled to limit the medical risk.

Some analysts said such a delay would change little in the Kremlin because Yeltsin, 65, had managed to balance the powers of all the potential rivals. Others disagreed, saying rivalry would increase and political instability would deepen.
"The longer the operation is put off, the more unstable the situation will be," Lyudmila Telen, deputy editor of the weekly newspaper Moscow News, told Reuters.
"No one is talking about coups d'etat or putsches, but we are talking about a time of troubles, without clear power divisions or collective responsiblity."

Other analysts said this could lead to inertia in decision- making which allowed problems, especially in the economy, to go unsolved. This, in turn, could encourage the communists to toughen their opposition to Yeltsin and the government.
Cardiac surgeon Renat Akchurin, who said in a television interview the operation could be delayed, said doctors would decide on the operation on Wednesday or Thursday.
Under Russia's constitution, the president has vast powers, overshadowing the government and parliament. If the president is absent, the balance of the whole political system can be upset.
Yeltsin has tried to create a balanced system around him by playing off the rivalries of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, security tsar Alexander Lebed and Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais.

Lebed, a 46-year-old former paratroop general, does not conceal his presidential ambitions and Chernomyrdin, 58, is a potential presidential rival. Chubais, 41, is an unlikely challenger but wants to consolidate his position in the Kremlin.

"The president has already been out of the Kremlin for a long time without any disasters happening. I don't think a delay in his operation will have a major effect now," said Viktor Borisyuk, until recently part of Yeltsin's team of analysts.

Alexander Golts, a comentator for the armed forces newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda, said he did not expect any big changes for the worse in the Kremlin and saw no risk of serious instablity in Yeltsin's extended absence. But he also predicted increased uncertainty and sounded a warning.

"I don't expect any cardinal changes. The president has carefully built up a political structure around him although, of course, a system built on a balance (of rivalries) can change as soon as the main 'balancer' disappears from the scene."
Some observers paint a more disturbing picture.

"We are facing troubled times. It is already hard to understand who answers for what in Russia and who is subordinate to whom," Yeltsin's former press secretary Pavel Voshchanov wrote recently in the daily newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda.
"But it is not the president's absence form the Kremlin that causes concern...It is another thing -- the palpable signs of an internal struggle (for power)."

Telen said she had welcomed the announcement on Thursday that Yeltsin would hand powers temporarily to Chernomyrdin for the duration of his operation. But she feared that decree would now be delayed or not implemented, prolonging uncertainty.

"Under the decree, powers will be clearly set out. Without it, power will be divided between the three -- Chernomyrdin, Chubais and Lebed -- and they will fight behind the scenes to get as much power for themselves as possible," she said.

Another fear is that a lack of clear divisions of power will lead to a failure to tackle major problems, particularly in the economy where a backlog of unpaid wages has already triggered some strikes and protests.

"We have to be prepared for a certain period of political impotence. Many things will not be dealt with and problems, especially in the social and financial areas, will just pile up," a Western diplomat said.
